\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large-scale LLM serving is increasingly shaped by the convergence of two trends that are independently effective but jointly challenging: sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) base models~\cite{todo:moe-llm} and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)-based multi-tenant serving~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. In production systems, these two trends naturally meet in \emph{multi-LoRA MoE serving}. While LoRA is widely used as a lightweight adaptation mechanism, existing multi-LoRA serving systems are typically not organized around expert-layer adaptation in sparse MoE models~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. Effectively customizing MoE models requires applying LoRA directly to the expert layers (MoE LoRA), as expert FFN blocks account for a large fraction of model capacity and are a natural target for task-specific adaptation~\cite{todo:moe-knowledge-capacity}. This setting is attractive because MoE reduces base-model compute, while MoE LoRA enables efficient per-tenant customization without replicating the full model. However, it also creates a new systems regime in which highly dynamic sparse expert routing~\cite{todo:moe-routing-dynamics} and long-tailed multi-adapter access~\cite{todo:slora} interact within the same execution pipeline.

This interaction is particularly problematic during the decode phase of prefill--decode deployments~\cite{todo:pd-serving}, where execution is latency-sensitive, operates at small effective batch sizes, and repeatedly performs routing and LoRA-related parameter access once per generated token. In pure MoE serving, the natural unit of management is the expert. In multi-LoRA serving, the unit is the adapter, and prior systems such as S-LoRA~\cite{todo:slora} and VaLoRA~\cite{mi2025empower} therefore adopt adapter-centric designs. In MoE + multi-LoRA decode, however, a request only needs the LoRA residual associated with the \emph{selected experts}, making the true unit of access and reuse a joint expert--LoRA object rather than an expert-only or adapter-only entity. This joint-object regime is further amplified by object size and memory pressure. Because expert layers are implemented as wide feed-forward blocks (FFNs)~\cite{todo:moe-ffn-architecture}, expert-layer LoRA modules are substantially larger than conventional attention-layer LoRAs. Coupled with the already large parameter footprint of the MoE base model~\cite{todo:large-moe-models}, this leaves only a limited GPU memory budget for expert--LoRA residency, enlarging and fragmenting the effective object space and making GPU residency harder to sustain under fixed memory budgets. More importantly, it exposes a fundamental systems mismatch: expert-centric abstractions fit pure MoE serving, and adapter-centric abstractions fit multi-LoRA serving, but neither matches expert--LoRA joint-object access in decode.

Our trace-driven case study, built on Azure LLM serving traces~\cite{zhang2021faster} with synthetic LoRA assignment, shows that this is not a marginal effect but a regime shift. Under joint-key modeling, the top 1000 objects account for only 40.7\% and 32.6\% of accesses under two adapter-mapping scenarios---independent and correlated assignment---compared to 89.1\% under expert-only modeling. Temporal locality degrades accordingly: the finite P99 reuse distance increases from 1,393 events to 2,041 and 4,521 events, while cold first touches rise from 1.0 to 9.7 and 13.6 per 10k events. These results show that multi-LoRA MoE serving does not merely enlarge the object space; it also fragments the effective working set and weakens temporal locality, making the access pattern substantially less cache-friendly.

These structural changes translate directly into system-level degradation under realistic cache budgets. With a shared 2048-object LRU cache, the miss rate increases from 0.00159 (expert-only) to 0.01095 and 0.01476 under joint-key modeling, a 6.9$\times$--9.3$\times$ increase. While the absolute miss rate remains low, these misses are highly skewed and concentrate on tail requests, where even a small number of misses directly dominate P99 latency. In this regime, performance is governed not by average miss rate, but by the worst-case accumulation of cold-object accesses. Synthetic control sweeps further show that the tail penalty emerges early and persists: at a fixed cache slice, the P99 latency proxy rises sharply as the number of LoRAs increases and quickly plateaus at a high level. At the request level, tail latency is dominated not by average degradation but by bursts of cold-object accesses: while an average request touches tens of cold objects, tail requests may touch hundreds to over a thousand. These findings suggest that cache misses in this regime are not rare anomalies but \emph{regime-driven tail events} concentrated on tail requests.

Once misses become a persistent feature of this regime, the conventional load-then-run paradigm becomes suboptimal. Existing GPU-centric systems treat a cache miss as a weight-migration problem, resolving it by transferring parameters from host to device before execution~\cite{todo:gpu-offload}. This approach works well for hot objects with predictable reuse, but breaks down for long-tail decode misses, where batches are small, reuse is uncertain, and host--device transfer latency is directly exposed on the critical path. As a result, the core systems bottleneck shifts from miss avoidance alone to \emph{miss handling}: the key question is no longer only how to keep more objects resident, but how unavoidable cold misses should be served.

This paper presents \textbf{COLoRA}, a decode-time serving runtime for multi-LoRA MoE models built around a \emph{hot/cold dual-path design} for expert--LoRA computation. Under expert--LoRA joint-object caching, working-set expansion and fragmentation make cold misses difficult to eliminate within practical GPU cache budgets. Rather than treating every miss as an immediate blocking \emph{promotion-first} recovery event, COLoRA adopts an \emph{execution-first} default: cache-hit objects continue on the GPU hot path, while cold misses are served through a CPU cold path to complete the current LoRA computation, and GPU promotion is deferred to future reuse. To make this design practical, COLoRA implements an optimized CPU cold path with AVX kernels and activation coalescing, enabling cold-miss handling to overlap with the GPU hot/base path in mixed hit/miss batches. COLoRA further includes a selective speculative dispatch extension for a subset of decode-time gate/up computation to expose additional overlap opportunities.

The key contributions of this work are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Problem characterization.} We identify the expert--LoRA joint-object regime in multi-LoRA MoE decode serving and show that working-set expansion and fragmentation make cold misses difficult to eliminate within realistic GPU cache budgets, turning miss handling---rather than cache capacity alone---into a first-order systems problem.

\item \textbf{Miss-handling abstraction.} We introduce a hot/cold dual-path serving design for expert--LoRA computation in decode. Its key abstraction change is to replace conventional \emph{promotion-first} load-then-run recovery with \emph{execution-first} recovery: hot objects remain on the GPU hot path, while cold misses are completed on a CPU cold path, and promotion is retained only for future reuse.

\item \textbf{System realization.} We implement an efficient CPU cold path with AVX kernels and activation coalescing, making execution-first handling practical under decode-time latency constraints and enabling overlap with the GPU hot/base path in mixed hit/miss batches.

\item \textbf{Extension for additional overlap.} We prototype a selective speculative dispatch mechanism for decode-time gate/up computation, using temporal locality and exact late binding to further expose overlap opportunities beyond the main miss-handling design.
\end{itemize}


\section{Background, Motivation, and Challenges}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{Background: Expert--LoRA Computation in Multi-LoRA MoE Decode}
\label{subsec:background}

We study decode-time serving where a shared sparse MoE base model is combined with multiple LoRA specializations. In this setting, each generated token still triggers dynamic expert routing in the base model, while different requests may invoke different LoRA adapters. As a result, the serving system must repeatedly determine not only which experts are activated, but also which adapter-specific LoRA states are needed on the latency-critical decode path.

This interaction changes the natural unit at which the system should reason about locality and misses. In dense multi-LoRA serving, adapter-level reasoning is often sufficient because accesses concentrate on a single adapter's weights. In MoE decode, however, each token activates only a small routed subset of experts, and LoRA computation is needed only for the routed experts of the current request. The relevant access unit is therefore not an expert or an adapter in isolation, but their joint occurrence in the decode path, which we refer to as an \emph{expert--LoRA joint object}.

This distinction matters particularly in decode. Decode operates at small effective batch sizes, repeats routing and parameter-access decisions once per token, and exposes miss-handling overheads directly on the latency-critical path. Consequently, when expert--LoRA joint objects do not fit cleanly within practical GPU cache budgets, the key systems question is not only how to manage residency, but also how to recover cold misses without inflating per-token latency.


\subsection{Motivation}
\label{subsec:motivation}

\subsubsection{Expert--LoRA Joint Objects as the Natural Access Unit}
\label{subsec:joint-object}

A central question is what abstraction the system should use to reason about locality, residency, and misses.

In dense models with a single adapter, adapter-level management is often sufficient because most tokens share the same adapted weights. In sparse MoE models, however, each token activates only a small routed subset of experts. Once multiple LoRA adapters coexist, accesses no longer concentrate on entire adapters or on experts alone, but on LoRA states attached to specific routed experts.

This makes expert--LoRA joint objects the natural access unit for decode-time serving. Adapter-level management is too coarse because it retains many unused expert slices together with the few that are actually needed. Expert-level management is incomplete because it ignores adapter diversity and therefore overestimates reuse across requests. To understand locality under multi-LoRA MoE serving, the relevant unit is thus not an expert or an adapter in isolation, but their joint occurrence on the decode path.

\subsubsection{Joint Objects Fragment Decode Locality}
\label{subsec:case-study}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{figures/fig1_popularity_rank.pdf}
  \includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{figures/fig2_reuse_distance.pdf}
  \caption{
  Joint expert--adapter modeling fundamentally degrades locality.\\
  (a) Popularity becomes significantly less concentrated: the top-1000 objects account for 89.1\% of accesses under expert-only modeling, but only 40.7\% and 32.6\% under joint modeling.\\
  (b) Temporal locality weakens: reuse distance increases substantially (P99: 1,393 $\rightarrow$ 2,041 $\rightarrow$ 4,521), and cold-start frequency rises sharply.\\
  Together, these results show that introducing the adapter dimension fragments both spatial and temporal locality, reducing the effectiveness of any bounded cache.
  }
  \label{fig:locality}
\end{figure*}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{figures/fig3_cache_curve.pdf}
  \includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{figures/fig5_tail_breakdown.pdf}
  \caption{
  Locality degradation directly translates into system-level inefficiency.\\
  (a) Under the same cache budget, miss rates increase significantly with joint modeling, showing that degraded locality cannot be compensated by fixed-capacity caching.\\
  (b) Tail requests access up to an order of magnitude more cold objects than average requests, concentrating misses in the tail.\\
  These results demonstrate that locality collapse not only increases average miss rate, but also amplifies tail latency.
  }
  \label{fig:system}
\end{figure*}

To examine whether this finer-grained view matters in practice, we perform a trace-driven replay study on a fixed MoE routing trace under three object definitions. \texttt{B0} uses expert-only keys $(\mathit{layer}, \mathit{expert})$. \texttt{B1} uses joint keys $(\mathit{layer}, \mathit{expert}, \mathit{adapter})$ with adapter identity sampled independently of expert routing. \texttt{B2} uses the same joint keys under correlated assignment, where certain adapters are more likely to co-occur with specific experts.

Figures~\ref{fig:locality} and~\ref{fig:system} reveal a consistent two-stage effect. Joint modeling first fragments decode locality; this locality loss then translates into higher miss rates and more severe tail behavior.

\paragraph{Popularity becomes less concentrated.}
As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:locality}(a), introducing the adapter dimension significantly flattens the popularity distribution. Under expert-only modeling, the top 1000 objects account for 89.1\% of accesses. Under joint modeling, this drops to 40.7\% and 32.6\%. The hot set therefore becomes much less dominant, reducing the effectiveness of any bounded GPU cache.

\paragraph{Temporal locality weakens, especially in the tail.}
Fig.~\ref{fig:locality}(b) shows that joint modeling substantially increases reuse distance and cold-start frequency. The P99 reuse distance grows from 1{,}393 to 2{,}041 and 4{,}521 events. These longer gaps are especially harmful in decode, where delayed reuse is less likely to be hidden or amortized, and where tail requests are more exposed to long-latency misses.

\paragraph{Locality loss amplifies misses and tail latency.}
As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:system}(a), miss rates rise significantly under the same cache budget once accesses are modeled jointly. More importantly, Fig.~\ref{fig:system}(b) shows that tail requests access up to an order of magnitude more cold objects than average requests. The degradation is therefore not limited to average miss rate: it is concentrated in the tail, where it directly amplifies request latency.

Taken together, these results suggest that the difficulty in multi-LoRA MoE decode serving is not merely insufficient cache capacity, but a deeper fragmentation of locality once expert access and adapter identity are considered jointly.

\subsection{Challenges}
\label{subsec:challenges}

The above observations reveal a fundamental shift in the role of caching. Under expert--LoRA joint-object modeling, locality degradation makes cold misses difficult to eliminate within practical GPU cache budgets. As a result, misses are no longer rare events that can be hidden behind a sufficiently large hot set; they become a dominant factor that must be explicitly managed on the latency-critical decode path.

This reframes the systems problem. The key question is no longer only how to reduce misses, but how to recover unavoidable misses without inflating per-token latency. Turning this insight into a practical runtime requires addressing three challenges.

\paragraph{Challenge 1: Organizing expert--LoRA objects under expanded and fragmented working sets.}
\label{subsec:challenge-residency}

Under joint-object modeling, the effective key space expands substantially, while reuse becomes weaker and more fragmented across requests. This makes coarse-grained management ineffective: adapter-level residency retains many expert slices that are never touched, whereas expert-only reasoning overestimates reuse by ignoring adapter diversity. At the same time, naively treating every expert--LoRA joint object as an independent cache unit can lead to unstable residency, repeated admissions of low-reuse objects, and excessive churn.

The system must therefore preserve the precision of joint-object reasoning without turning fine-grained residency into a self-defeating management problem. In other words, it must organize expert--LoRA objects at the granularity demanded by actual computation, while preventing limited GPU cache capacity from being consumed by transient cold objects.

\paragraph{Challenge 2: Recovering cold misses without forcing promotion-first stalls on decode.}
\label{subsec:challenge-miss}

In this regime, many misses correspond to cold objects whose reuse is too limited to amortize the cost of immediate promotion. If the system continues to apply a conventional load-then-run policy, each such miss becomes a blocking recovery event: the current token must wait for weight migration before expert--LoRA computation can proceed. Under decode-time latency sensitivity, this directly amplifies tail latency.

The system therefore needs a different default recovery strategy for cold misses. Instead of forcing all misses through immediate GPU promotion, it must provide a way to complete the current expert--LoRA computation without making promotion the only recovery path, while still preserving the option to promote objects later when future reuse justifies it.

\paragraph{Challenge 3: Making cold-path recovery practical and overlap-friendly under decode constraints.}
\label{subsec:challenge-overlap}

Changing the miss-recovery abstraction is not sufficient by itself. If cold-path execution is too slow, the system merely replaces GPU promotion stall with CPU-side stall. If it is poorly integrated with the decode pipeline, heterogeneous execution introduces a new source of queueing and tail behavior rather than alleviating the original one.

The system must therefore make cold-path recovery efficient enough to operate at small, irregular decode batch sizes, and organize execution so that cold-miss handling can overlap with GPU hot-path and base-model computation whenever dependencies allow. The challenge is not only to provide an alternative path, but to ensure that this path reduces exposed miss latency instead of becoming a new bottleneck.

\section{Design}
\label{sec:design-overview}

\subsection{Core Idea}
\label{subsec:core-idea}

Under joint-object modeling, cache misses become unavoidable and latency-critical, requiring explicit miss handling rather than relying on caching to hide them.

These observations shift the problem from data placement to execution-path selection: instead of always blocking on promotion, the system must decide whether to serve a miss immediately from the cold layer or to invest in future reuse through promotion.

This shift imposes three constraints: (1) maintaining a precise hot set without inducing churn, (2) handling misses without blocking the critical decode path, and (3) overlapping heterogeneous execution so that miss handling does not become the new tail bottleneck.

COLoRA satisfies these constraints through three mechanisms: selective joint-object residency, non-blocking miss handling with a cold-layer execution path, and overlap-aware heterogeneous execution.

\subsection{Selective Joint-Object Residency}
\label{subsec:memory-hierarchy}

COLoRA maintains a stable hot set by selectively promoting joint objects while suppressing low-value cache churn.

To address Challenge~\ref{subsec:challenge-residency}, COLoRA uses an asymmetric memory hierarchy: GPU memory serves as a bounded hot cache for reusable joint objects, while CPU memory maintains a full read-only replica that acts as both the cold layer and the execution source for misses.

Flattened popularity under joint-object modeling weakens hot-set dominance, making naive fine-grained caching unstable. Without filtering, frequent insertions of low-reuse objects lead to repeated eviction and re-admission, degenerating into churn.

COLoRA therefore performs selective promotion. Each joint object maintains lightweight utility signals derived from recent accesses, and promotion is gated by minimum-hit thresholds, bounded queues, and cooldown windows. This preserves fine-grained precision while preventing promotion traffic from overwhelming the system.

\subsection{Non-Blocking Miss Handling}
\label{subsec:cpu-first}

COLoRA serves misses without blocking the decode path by executing directly from the cold layer.

To address Challenge~\ref{subsec:challenge-miss}, COLoRA avoids blocking on promotion for low-reuse objects. Under degraded temporal locality, many misses correspond to objects whose reuse is too distant to amortize promotion cost. In this regime, blocking load-then-run exposes promotion latency directly on the critical path.

COLoRA instead serves misses immediately. When a joint object misses in the GPU cache, the request is routed to a cold-layer execution path rather than waiting for promotion. Promotion is treated as an asynchronous optimization for future requests rather than a prerequisite for serving the current one.

The dense expert backbone remains on GPU, while only the sparse LoRA residual uses the heterogeneous path. This confines miss handling to the component responsible for fragmentation, minimizing disruption to the main execution flow.

\subsection{Analytical Regime for Non-Blocking Miss Handling}
\label{subsec:analytical-model}

We use a lightweight latency model to characterize the regime in which non-blocking fallback reduces the exposed critical-path latency of a miss relative to blocking GPU promotion.

Consider a miss on joint object $j$, where $W_j$ denotes the missed weight size and $A_j, O_j$ denote the activation and output sizes of the fallback path. In decode, batch sizes are small and sequence length is typically one, so $A_j$ and $O_j$ scale with per-token activations, whereas $W_j$ scales with the missed object weights.

The exposed latency of the blocking promotion path is
\begin{equation}
T_{\mathrm{block}}(j)
=
T_{\mathrm{xfer}}^{w}(j)
+
T_{\mathrm{gpu}}(j)
+
T_{\mathrm{stall}}(j),
\label{eq:blocking-path}
\end{equation}
where $T_{\mathrm{xfer}}^{w}(j)$ is the host-to-device weight transfer cost, $T_{\mathrm{gpu}}(j)$ is the GPU execution cost after promotion, and $T_{\mathrm{stall}}(j)$ is the blocking-side delay exposed on the critical path, including queueing, synchronization, and promotion-side cache-management overheads when they lie on the critical path.

\begin{equation}
T_{\mathrm{fb}}(j)
=
T_{\mathrm{xfer}}^{a}(j)
+
T_{\mathrm{cpu}}(j)
+
T_{\mathrm{merge}}(j)
-
T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(j),
\label{eq:fallback-path}
\end{equation}
where $T_{\mathrm{xfer}}^{a}(j)$ is the activation-side transfer cost, including activation transfer and result return, $T_{\mathrm{cpu}}(j)$ is the CPU execution cost including dispatch and kernel wake-up overheads, $T_{\mathrm{merge}}(j)$ is the rejoin overhead, and $T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(j)$ is the portion hidden under independent GPU work.

COLoRA prefers fallback when
\begin{equation}
T_{\mathrm{fb}}(j) < T_{\mathrm{block}}(j).
\label{eq:fallback-better}
\end{equation}

We approximate the transfer terms as
\begin{align}
T_{\mathrm{xfer}}^{w}(j)
&\approx
\alpha + \frac{W_j}{B_{\mathrm{pcie}}}, \\
T_{\mathrm{xfer}}^{a}(j)
&\approx
2\alpha + \frac{A_j + O_j}{B_{\mathrm{pcie}}},
\label{eq:transfer-model}
\end{align}
where $\alpha$ is the fixed host-device transfer overhead and $B_{\mathrm{pcie}}$ is the effective transfer bandwidth.

Raw transfer cost alone does not necessarily favor fallback, since activation-side service incurs a round-trip transfer whereas promotion transfers weights only once. COLoRA instead targets the regime in which blocking-side delay and overlap effects dominate the exposed latency of a cold miss.

Substituting the transfer terms, fallback is favored when
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\bigl(T_{\mathrm{xfer}}^{a}(j) - T_{\mathrm{xfer}}^{w}(j)\bigr)
+ \bigl(T_{\mathrm{cpu}}(j) - T_{\mathrm{gpu}}(j)\bigr) \\
+ T_{\mathrm{merge}}(j)
- T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(j)
- T_{\mathrm{stall}}(j)
< 0 .
\end{split}
\label{eq:decode-regime}
\end{equation}

Equation~\ref{eq:decode-regime} characterizes the regime targeted by COLoRA: cold misses with weak near-term reuse, where blocking promotion exposes cost immediately while deferring benefit to future requests, whereas fallback serves the current miss directly and may additionally hide part of its cost through overlap. COLoRA therefore requires only lower \emph{exposed} latency than blocking promotion, not lower raw compute latency than GPU execution.

\subsection{Low-Overhead Miss Execution Path}
\label{subsec:cpu-fallback}

COLoRA ensures that the fallback path is efficient enough to make non-blocking miss handling viable in the decode regime.

Decode misses are small, irregular, and latency-sensitive, making generic framework execution inefficient due to high fixed overhead. COLoRA therefore implements a specialized execution path tailored to this regime.

Miss work is grouped by adapter, lightweight kernels are used when available, and the control path is kept compact. The implementation exposes AVX-512 BF16 kernels for the gate, up, and down projections, reducing dispatch overhead and improving efficiency for small tensor shapes.

The goal is not to outperform GPU execution in general, but to ensure that for cold, low-reuse objects, fallback incurs lower exposed miss latency than blocking promotion.

\subsection{Overlap-Aware Heterogeneous Execution}
\label{subsec:overlap}

COLoRA overlaps GPU execution with miss handling to reduce the exposed cost of heterogeneous execution and prevent fallback from becoming a new tail bottleneck.

To address Challenge~\ref{subsec:challenge-overlap}, COLoRA exploits mixed batches containing both GPU-cache hits and misses. Without overlap, non-blocking miss handling degenerates into a serialized pipeline, where the fallback path becomes the new critical path.

COLoRA launches miss execution asynchronously when independent GPU work is available and synchronizes only when the residual output is required. This allows CPU computation, GPU computation, and data movement to proceed concurrently.

The runtime also tracks signals such as promotion queue depth, CPU queue depth, queueing delay, and overlap ratio, enabling the system to remain explainable and to identify when contention or insufficient overlap limits performance.

\subsection{Behavior Under Different Locality Regimes}
\label{subsec:graceful-degradation}

COLoRA adapts to workload locality rather than enforcing heterogeneity.

When locality is strong and the working set fits in GPU memory, most requests hit in the hot cache and execution behaves similarly to a GPU-only system. As locality degrades and misses become frequent, the system transitions to heterogeneous execution, using non-blocking miss handling and overlap to stabilize tail latency.

This adaptive behavior ensures that COLoRA improves performance in fragmented regimes while remaining efficient in well-behaved workloads.
